background.definition: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease of unknown etiology, with protean manifestations and variable courses and prognoses, characterized by arrays of antibodies directed against specific molecules of nuclei (native DNA antigens) and cytoplasm, in association with cell-mediated autoimmunity.

list.listitem: According to population-based administrative databases, the incidence of SLE is approximately 3 per 100,000 persons per year (95% CI, 2.6-3.4).
In the 3rd National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, the prevalence of SLE in adults older than 17 years, based on self-reported physician diagnosis, was 241 per 100,000 (95% CI, 130-352).
The prevalence in women is approximately 100 per 100,000 population (95% CI, 20-180).
Approximately 90% of patients with SLE are women.

Polyautoimmunity (combinations of autoimmune disease) is common in patients with SLE, in one cross sectional study of 335 patients with SLE in Columbia, 41% had at least one other autoimmune disease, most commonly autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD), antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) and Sjögren's syndrome.
SLE is a multifactorial disease resulting from the combination of genetic and environmental factors.

Evidence of genetic predisposition in humans comes from twin studies. In a study of twins with one of the pair with SLE, no dizygotic twin had SLE, while as many as one third of monozygotic twins were concordant for lupus.

Approximately 4% to 5% of patients with SLE have family members with lupus. Also, approximately 10% of patients with SLE have relatives with other autoimmune disorders. Additionally, the familial aggregation factor for siblings was between 6 and 20 (the higher the number, the stronger the familial link).
Important suspected environmental factors include ultraviolet B, radiation exposure, infections, emotional stress, surgery, and pregnancy.
Histocompatibility genes involved in SLE include HLA-B8, DRB1, DR2, DR3 and DR4, and homozygous deficiencies of early complement components (C2, C4).
Nonhistocompatibility genes are also involved (eg, C1q, Fc-gamma-receptor IIA and IIIA, and mannose-binding ligand polymorphisms in chromosome 10).

External factors introduce their own antigens to be processed by antigen-presenting cells (APC), and they cause apoptosis (intrinsically programmed cell death) of host cells, thus releasing self-antigens (DNA).
These self-antigens are in turn processed by APCs with the activation of B and T lymphocytes, which produce antibodies and cell-mediated cytotoxicity, respectively.
Ultimately, there is end-organ damage, mediated by humoral mechanisms (circulating immune-complexes) and cellular autoimmunity.

Because they are at higher risk for developing coronary artery disease than the general population, patients with SLE should especially be encouraged to quit smoking, control their blood pressure, and control their lipids. C

Patients taking corticosteroids are at an increased risk of developing osteoporotic fractures. Although calcitonin, calcium plus vitamin D, and bisphosphonates all prevent bone loss as measured by bone mineral density, there is no evidence that they decrease fracture rates in this population. B

Low dose aspirin is recommended for patients with SLE and antiphospholipid antibodies to prevent thrombotic events; an RCT with 166 patients found that adding low intensity warfarin does not improve outcomes. B
Pneumococcal vaccine is safe and recommended for patients with SLE. Sequential vaccination with 7 valent followed by 23 valent vaccines does not offer any advantage in patients with SLE.B

Suspect SLE in patients with arthralgias; general symptoms, such as fever or fatigue; and symptoms or signs of multiple system illness such as unexplained lymphadenopathy, inflammatory arthritis, glomerulonephritis, or interstitial lung disease. C
Most people with a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) do not have SLE; a positive ANA in the absence of other clinical criteria is insufficient to establish a diagnosis of SLE. C
Apply the 2012 SLIC classsification criteria for SLE (). Once clinical suspicion for SLE is high, proceed with specific serologic tests.B

list.listitem: Apply the 2012 SLICC classification criteria ().

The most frequent presenting symptom in patients with SLE is joint pain, which may be associated with constitutional symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss, or fever. Approximately one third of patients have oral ulcers, and between 20% and 40% have pleurisy. Most symptoms are specific (ie, malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, renal problems, seizures), but lack sensitivity, and therefore, overall accuracy.

Approximately 50% of patients with lupus have skin manifestations. Cutaneous lesions in SLE include the classic malar or "butterfly" rash, triggered by UVB radiation, and may precede systemic manifestations.
Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is a nonscarring form of lupus which affects upper extremities and torso, sparing the face.
The lesions of discoid lupus erythematosus are disfiguring and can progress with scarring and central atrophy.
Raynaud's phenomenon is a nonspecific manifestation that may occur alone or associated with SLE or other connective tissue diseases.
Among patients with SLE who develop acute psychosis, approximately 60% do so within the first year of diagnosis. Psychosis may be triggered by high doses of prednisone.

Many drugs (including procainamide, isoniazid, hydralazine, minocycline, tumor necrosis factor alpha blockers, and statins) can cause a lupuslike syndrome that abates once the offending agent is removed.

Approximately one third of healthy individuals have a positive ANA at a dilution of 1:40, and the test result is commonly abnormal in other collagen vascular diseases. Thus, an abnormal ANA result, even in a patient with nonspecific joint pain, is not necessarily diagnostic of SLE.

When suspected based on clinical symptoms and an elevated ANA, order anti-dsDNA and antiSm antibodies to confirm the diagnosis. Use of anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies is not recommended for diagnostic confirmation, although they should be obtained in women who are planning pregnancy or have an unplanned pregnancy.
Anti-ds DNA is less sensitive but more specific than ANA, but decreases in levels are associated with flares and precedes nephritis.
Antiribosomal P antibodies were found in 18 of 20 patients with psychosis due to lupus.
Antihistone antibodies are seen in drug-induced lupus, although they may be present in idiopathic lupus.
Approximately 50% of patients with SLE have renal manifestations (from urinary casts and proteinuria to end-stage renal disease).Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia may also be seen.

Patients may have anemia of chronic disease, iron-deficiency anemia, or autoimmune hemolytic anemia of the warm-type (IgG antibodies react to red blood cells at 37 degrees C). Thrombocytopenia is usually secondary to idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura.
Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is frequently associated with SLE. In a cohort of 1000 patients with APS, approximately one third had SLE.
Ultrasound is a valid and reproducible tool for diagnosing synovitis in patients with inflammatory arthritis.
24 hour urine for protein and serum creatinine and the protein/creatinine ratio in an early morning urine sample are recommended to assess for lupus nephropathy.
Suspect SLE in patients with arthralgias; general symptoms, such as fever or fatigue; and symptoms or signs of multiple system illness.
Initial testing should include complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein, ANA, and a urinalysis.
Apply the 2012 SLICC classification criteria ().
The treatment target of SLE should be remission (or achieving lowest possible disease activity) of systemic symptoms and organ manifestations. C
Mild disease: For patients with musculoskeletal and/or skin disease without evidence of organ damage, treated treat with NSAIDs and antimalarials. B
Moderate disease activity and non-renal SLE: These patients should receive methotrexate.B
Severe non-renal disease: IV cyclophosphamide is recommended.B

Antimalarial drugs are recommended for all patients with SLE who do not have contraindications, with hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine the preferred therapies. The monoclonal antibody belimumab should be reserved for patients with active SLE who do not respond to these therapies. Immunoglobulins may be considered when patients have severe thrombocytopenia and either bleeding or requiring surgery.B
More severe disease should be treated with systemic steroids and immunosuppressants (either as primary treatment of the organ-specific manifestation or as steroid-sparing agents). B
Patients typically experience 0.1 to 1.8 flares per year, based on a review of the literature.

Treatment overview: EULAR task force recommends use of immunosuppresion with methpotrexate or azathioprine in patients with non-renal SLE with moderate disease activity. For patients with severe non-renal disease, IV cyclophosphamide is recommended. Antimalarial drugs are recommended for all patients with SLE who do not have contraindications, with hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine being the preferred therapies. When using glucocorticoids for treatment of lupus, try to keep the dose of prednisone below 30 mg/day. The monoclonal antibody belimumab should be reserved for patients with active SLE with skin/joint involvment who do not respond to these therapies. Immunoglobulins may be considered when patients have severe thrombocytopenia and either bleeding or requiring surgery. Treat to target recommendations have been developed targetting remission, preventing organ damage and improving quality of life.

There are very few randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of antimalarials (such as hydroxychloroquine) or corticosteroids despite their widespread use and guidelines recommending their use as part of the general management of patients with SLE.

In one RCT of 71 patients with mild SLE who required low-dose prednisone, patients taking hydroxychloroquine had the same rate of remission as patients taking placebo. Patients taking hydroxychloroquine had lower pain scores, but all other measures were similar.

In a variation of the traditional RCT, 47 patients with clinically stable SLE already taking hydroxychloroquine were randomized to withdrawal of medication (using a placebo) or continuation. After 6 months, only 9 of the 25 patients maintained on hydroxychloroquine had flare-ups of SLE compared with 16 of the 22 patients in the withdrawal group. Additionally, only 1 of the 25 patients using active therapy had severe flare-ups compared with 5 of the 22 withdrawn patients. However, after 3 years of follow up, there were no statistically significant differences in flare-ups or hospitalizations.

An RCT of 103 patients with cutaneous lupus erythematosus found that hydroxychloroquine was more effective than placebo at improving investigator assessed improvement and measures of disease severity.

A systematic review of 95 articles including RCTs and observational studies concluded that evidence was strong that anti-malarials prevent lupus flares and increase long-term survival; there was moderate evidence of protection against irreversible organ damage, thrombosis and bone mass loss. In pregnancy women, evidence was again deemed strong that anti-malarials, particularly hydroxychloroquine, decreases lupus activity without adverse fetal effects.

A RCT of 46 patients with clinically stable SLE but who had rising anti-ds DNA titers, only 2 of 22 patients taking prednisone (30 mg/day tapered off over 18 weeks) had a flare up compared with 20 of the 24 treated with usual care. Seven of the control patients required cytotoxic therapy compared with only 2 of the patients on prednisone.

In a similar RCT, of the 41 patients with clinically stable SLE but rising anti-ds DNA titers, none of the patients taking prednisone (30 mg/day for 2 weeks, 20 mg/day for 1 week, or 10 mg/day for 1 week) had a severe flare-up within 90 days compared with 6 of the 20 patients taking placebo.

Therapies for severe, organ-specific manifestations consist of glucocorticoids either alone or in combination with immunosuppressant drugs. Glucocorticoid dosages vary with disease severity. Oral glucocorticoids may be given at very high doses (1-2 mg/kg/d), high doses (0.6-1 mg/kg/d), low doses (0.125-0.5 mg/kg/d) or very low doses (<0.125 mg/kg/d).

The human monoclonal antibody belimumab has been shown to increase the time to severe disease flares compared with placebo (171 vs 118 days, HR 0.51, 95% CI, 0.35-0.74) and there was a trend toward allowing more patients to significantly reduce their corticosteroid dosage (18% vs 12%, OR 1.7, 95% CI, 0.95-2.8). Other studies have confirmed this benefit.
An RCT with 166 patients with moderate to severe disease activity found a greater response rate among those given ustekinumab vs placebo (62% vs 33%, NNT = 3).

A study of anifrollumab in patients with moderate to severe SLE found a greater likelihood of treatment response (the primary outcome) in those receiving active drug (34% vs 17%, p = 0.01, NNT = 6). Infections such as herpes zoster (10% vs 2%) and influenza (8% vs 2%) were more common with the drug, though.

A dose ranging study with 314 patients found improvement in signs and symptoms with 4 mg ( but not 2 mg) baricitinib compared wo placebo. Risk of serious infections was higher with baricitinib (6% vs 1%).

A systematic review identified 28 studies of monoclonal antibotides for patients with SLE. Only belimumab met its primary clinical endpoint, and is recommended for patients with active SLE who have not responded to standard therapy. The remainder achieved some improvements in secondary outcomes, and were potentially steroid sparing, but did not achieve their primary endpoint. Adverse events led to the early termination of several trials.

The anti-CD20 antibody rituximab has been used in patients with serious organ system involvment that has not responded to standard therapies. Data regarding its efficacy is limited to uncontrolled observational studies.

Telitacicept modulates b-cell function. A trial randomized 335 persons with active SLE to telitacicept or placebo. A clinical response on a modified SRI-4 symptom scale was significantly greater for the active treatment group (67% vs 33%, p < 0.001) NNT = 3). Adverse events occuring more frequently in the treatment (NNH=4) include respiratory infections, reduced IgG and IgM levels, and injection site reactions.

Induction treatment of proliferative glomerulonephritis consists of high-dose glucocorticoid therapy in combination with either IV cyclophosphamide (CYC) (0.5-1 g/m2 BSA) monthly for 6 months followed by quarterly doses, or mycophenolate mofetil (MMF).

Mycophenolate has emerged as first line immunosuppressive agent for induction therapy in lupus nephritis. It has been shown to be non-inferior in efficacy compared to cyclophosphamide with fewer adverse effects. A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs, concluded that efficacy, risk of death, and rates of renal failure were comparable to CYC, but fewer patients developed amenorrhea and leukopenia. IV cyclophosphamide remains the drug of choice for very severe cases and life threatening disease.

In a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs comparing MMF with CYC in 268 patients with severe lupus nephritis, MMF was more effective than CYC in achieving remission (65% vs 48%; number needed to treat = 6; 95% CI, 4-311). Although few patients taking MMF died or developed end-stage renal disease (3% and 4%, respectively) compared with CYC (10% for each), the numbers were small and not statistically significant.

During 6 years of follow up, azathioprine and MMF were more effective at preventing death than CYC (0%, 5%, and 20%, respectively) and chronic renal failure (5%, 5%, and 15%, respectively) when used as maintenance therapy in patients with lupus nephritis.
Following induction therapy, atleast 3 years of maintenance immunosuppressive therapy is recommended to optimise outcomes.
Central nervous system (transverse myelitis or central nervous system vasculitis) therapy consists of high-dose steroids in combination with steroid-sparing agents, such as CYC.
The data are too limited to determine if corticosteroids are more effective than CYC in treating patients with neuropsychiatric lupus.

See a separate chapter on discoid lupus. A Cochrane review of medical therapy for discoid lupus erythematosus identified 5 trials with 197 patients. They concluded that fluocinonide cream may be more effective than hydrocortisone, and that acitretin and hydroxychloroquine are similarly effective.

A guideline from the ACR and American Society of Hip and Knee Surgeons provides guidance about medication use perioperatively for patients with rheumatic diseases. They recommend continuing methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide, and doxycycline. They also recommend continuing mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, cyclosporine, and tacrolimus for patients with severe SLE, while witholding them for patients with non-severe SLE.

Regarding biologic agents (monoclonal antibodies), they should be stopped and surgery scheduled at the end of the next dosing cycle. The drug should only be restarted post-operatively when 2 weeks have elapsed, and only in patients without complications or infections or poor wound healing.

Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), a naturally occurring inactive steroid, may be effective in improving short-term quality of life in patients with mild to moderate SLE. Impact on disease activity was inconstant but most studies showed no benefit.
A small study with 68 patients randomized them to green tea extract (two 1000 mg capsules daily) or placebo and after 12 weeks found improvements in quality of life.

Based on a systematic review of 6 studies with 290 patients with SLE, patients performing low-impact aerobic exercises that gradually increased in intensity, duration, and frequency showed a larger reduction in fatigue scores than control patients.

In a small study of 183 women with SLE, the annual rate of flares in women taking oral contraceptives was similar to those taking placebo (slightly less than 8% per year). However, women with positive antiphospholipid antibodies may not be good candidates for combined hormonal contraception given their elevated baseline risk of thrombosis.
Transitional care improves outcomes compared with usual care in patients with SLE.

Since the prevalence of SLE is so low, most primary care physicians will not have much experience managing moderate or severe disease. The American College of Rheumatology recommends that patients be referred to a rheumatologist to establish or confirm the diagnosis, to assess disease activity and severity, to provide general disease management, and to manage uncontrolled, severe, or complicated disease.
Patients with mild, stable disease can be managed by primary care physicians.
The rheumatologist should help the primary care physician by establishing a plan of care, including guidelines for monitoring, treatment, and referral.

Consider hospitalization in patients with SLE who have high or persistent fever, chills; those with acute abdominal pain, severe anemia or thrombocytopenia, or evidence of bleeding; and any patients with psychosis, persistent seizures, or focal neurologic signs.

Finally, patients with SLE should be hospitalized if they have chest pain, new or worsening dyspnea, worsening or severe nephritis (anasarca, hematuria, hypertension, marked proteinuria, presence of cellular casts in urine), or any suspicion of an acute thrombotic event.

Indications for renal biopsy to diagnose lupus nephritis include increasing serum creatinine without an obvious cause, proteinuria (≥1.0 gm/24 hr), proteinuria ≥0.5 gm/24 hr plus the presence of either casts or ≥5 RBC/HPF in the urine. Classification should utilize the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society criteria: Class I or II: no treatment needed Class III or IV: aggressive treatment with glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents. Class V: mycophenolate mofetil 2 to 3 gm total daily orally OR IV cyclophosphamide + glucocorticoids Class VI: prepare patient for renal replacement therapy
Adjunctive treatments include hydroxychloroquine, hypertension should be controlled, and they should take an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
Renal manifestations are more severe in Hispanic and African American populations. B
In a large prospective cohort of patients with SLE, the overall cumulative probability of survival after disease diagnosis at 5, 10, 15, and 20 years was 95%, 91%, 85%, and 78%, respectively. B
Patients with SLE should be evaluated regularly for any clinical, laboratory, and/or serologic evidence of disease activity or worsening of preexisting disease. C
SLE may follow a relapsing-remitting course, go into remission, or progress with high disease activity, marked morbidity, and even death.
In a large prospective cohort of patients with SLE, the overall cumulative probability of survival after disease diagnosis at 5, 10, 15, and 20 years was 95%, 91%, 85%, and 78%, respectively.
In a longitudinal study of 53 patients with SLE, increased hematologic and renal activity was associated with a decreased C3 [OR = 1.6; 95% CI, 1.1-3.1] and C4 [OR = 2.9; 95% CI, 1.3-3.6].
Patients with SLE who also have antiphospholipid antibodies are at increased risk of venous thromboembolic events and pregnancy loss.
In the LUMINA study, after 6 months of follow-up of patients with SLE, 14% of white patients, 43% of Hispanic patients, and 51% of African American patients developed lupus nephritis.
In the LUMINA study, permanent organ damage accrued more rapidly in Hispanic patients than in white or African American patients.
Hypertension, high serum creatinine, and a high lupus nephritis chronicity score are associated with an increased risk of chronic renal failure and death in patients with lupus nephritis.

In a case control study, atherosclerosis (based on the presence of sonographically detected carotid plaque) was present in approximately one third of SLE patients and only 15% of control patients. Independent of traditional risk factors for coronary artery disease, patients with SLE are at high risk for myocardial infarction, even in patients younger than 35 years.
Lifelong monitoring is required for most patients.
Patients with mild, stable disease should be seen every 3 to 6 months.
Patients with severe disease, active disease, or with medication complications should be seen more frequently.
At routine follow-up visits, obtain a complete blood count with differential, platelet count, serum creatinine measurement, and urinalysis, even if the patient had normal values in the past.

Patients with known renal disease should have a urinalysis, 24-hour urine collection for protein, creatinine measurement, complete blood count, and determination of cholesterol, calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, sodium, and potassium levels approximately once a month at the onset of nephritis—more often if the condition is unstable.
It is also useful to measure serum complement levels (C3/C4) and anti-ds DNA Ab at regular intervals.
During follow-up visits, assess signs and symptoms of depression or psychosis.
Patients taking hydroxychloroquine need to have an annual retinal examination by an ophthalmologist.
Pregnant women with SLE are considered high risk and should be referred to the appropriate level of obstetric care.

Among 203 women with SLE who became pregnant 267 times, only 86% had live births, of which approximately half were full term. Among the women with highly active SLE only 77% had live births, 26% of which were full term.
Nearly 60% of women with active SLE who become pregnant had increased disease activity during pregnancy compared with only 8% whose disease was quiescent before pregnancy.
In a prospective cohort of 100 pregnant women with anti-Ro/SSA and connective tissue disease, the risk of developing heart block in offspring was 2% (95% CI, 0.5%-7%) in first observed pregnancies.

In a small RCT of 20 pregnant women with SLE, 3 of the 10 women taking placebo had flare-ups compared with 1 woman taking hydroxychloroquine. Three women, all taking placebo, developed toxemia. One fetal death occurred (in a woman taking placebo who had developed toxemia).

feature.caption: SLICC criteria for diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus. Patients must have at least four criteria (including one clinical and one immunologic criterion, or they must have lupus nephritis as the sole clinical criterion in the presence of either ANA or anti-dsDNA antibodies.

tr.td: 5. Synovitis in 2 or more joints, with swelling or effusion OR tenderness in 2 or more joints, and 30+ minutes morning stiffness.

2. Anti-dsDNA elevated (if ELiSA must be 2x above upper limit normal)
